meaning: Of unmeasured splendour; infinite light; the Buddha of the Pure Land Sukhāvatī.

pronunciation.note: Amitābha is Tier 1 because the medial ā is long. The name is a standard Sanskrit bahuvrīhi compound: a-mita ('unmeasured') + ābha ('light, splendor'). In East Asian Buddhism he is also known as Amitāyus, 'Infinite Life,' the two names emphasizing light and longevity.

domains.title: Buddha of Infinite Light
domains.subtitle: Pure Land, Compassion, and Other-Power Salvation
domains.lead: Amitābha is the Buddha whose light has no limit and whose compassion refuses no one. In Mahāyāna Buddhism he presides over Sukhāvatī, the Blissful Land, a western paradise where rebirth guarantees progress toward Buddhahood — and his cult transformed Buddhism from a monastic path of self-cultivation into a devotional religion open to laypeople, sinners, and the spiritually exhausted.

cards.name: Sukhāvatī
cards.desc: The Pure Land of Bliss: gold trees, jeweled ponds, and ceaseless Dharma teaching — a Buddha-field built as a gift.

cards.name: The Forty-Eight Vows
cards.desc: As the monk Dharmākara he vowed that even those with heavy karma could be reborn in Sukhāvatī through faith and name-recitation.

cards.name: Nembutsu / Niànfó
cards.desc: The invocation of his name — Namo Amitābhāya, Namo Amituofo — becomes the central practice of Pure Land devotion.

cards.name: Welcoming Descent
cards.desc: At death he descends with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to escort the faithful — the raigō painted and meditated upon across East Asia.

mythology.lead: Amitābha's mythology is the story of a vow. Long ago, as the monk Dharmākara, he stood before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and promised to build a Buddha-field so perfect that any being who trusted in him would be reborn there and swiftly attain enlightenment — and then he practiced until the promise became the cosmos.

myths.title: The Vows of Dharmākara
myths.text: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra — the longer of the three Pure Land sūtras, carried into Chinese more than once between the second and fifth centuries — describes how the monk Dharmākara, after five aeons of contemplation, surveyed every Buddha-field in the ten directions and distilled from their best qualities forty-six vows: forty-eight in the Chinese recensions, forty-six in the surviving Sanskrit. The eighteenth vow became the foundation of Pure Land practice: any being, however burdened by karma, who entrusted themselves to him and called his name even ten times would be reborn in Sukhāvatī. Having made the vows, Dharmākara labored through countless ages until every one stood fulfilled, and he became Amitābha, the Buddha of Infinite Light, his Pure Land lying to the west of every world that needs it. The sūtra's claim is quiet and enormous: salvation is not a prize for the strong but a gift finished long ago, waiting only to be received.

myths.title: Vaidehī's Sixteen Contemplations
myths.text: The Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra is addressed to Queen Vaidehī, imprisoned by her own son, the patricide Ajātaśatru, in the palace where the Buddha's great disciple had already been starved nearly to death. In her despair she begged the Buddha for a land without sorrow, and the Buddha, appearing in her cell, taught sixteen graded contemplations — from the setting sun to the jeweled trees, waters, and throne of Sukhāvatī — culminating in a vision of Amitābha himself. The sūtra then makes its most radical move: even one who has committed the five gravest sins, if at the moment of death they sincerely call Amitābha's name, will be received. Composed later than the other Pure Land sūtras, it is the devotional manual that carried the cult to the laity: vision first, ethics after, and mercy down to the final breath.

myths.title: The Lord of Sukhāvatī in the Lotus Cosmos
myths.text: The Saddharma-puṇḍarīka Sūtra (Lotus Sūtra) places Amitābha within a cosmos crowded with Buddhas rather than a universe with one savior. In its eleventh chapter the assembly beholds an immense jeweled stūpa rising from the earth, and within it the Buddha Prabhūtaratna — Many Treasures — who confirms every Buddha's teaching; to open that stūpa, the Buddha summons manifestations of himself from every direction, including the Amitābha of the western Sukhāvatī. The sūtra's twenty-fifth chapter then locates Avalokiteśvara — the bodhisattva who answers every cry — in Amitābha's Pure Land, sent from that western paradise to the worlds of the east, so that Amitābha's compassion travels in person. The pairing became permanent in art and liturgy: the Buddha who promises the land, and the bodhisattva who comes back from it to fetch the promise's beneficiaries. The Lotus thus makes Sukhāvatī not an escape hatch from the Buddhist cosmos but one of its busiest stations.

myths.title: The First Pure Land Society
myths.text: The devotional movement that would conquer East Asia began as a club on a mountain. In 402 CE the monk Huiyuan — the great exegete, recently settled at Donglin monastery on Mount Lushan — gathered one hundred and twenty-three lay and monastic companions before an image of Amitābha and led them in a joint vow to be reborn together in Sukhāvatī; their names were inscribed in stone as a contract with the Buddha. His biography in Hui Jiao's Gaoseng zhuan records the society as the model of lay Pure Land devotion, and later tradition crowned Huiyuan the movement's first patriarch. The gesture proved prophetic: what was done once on Lushan as an elite experiment among scholars would, eight centuries later, be repeated in every Japanese village — the Buddha's name as a shared vow, recited together by people who would never meet again except, they trusted, in the Pure Land.

lore.syncretism: Amitābha became the central figure of Pure Land Buddhism in China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam — Ēmítuófó, Amit'a, Amida, A Di Đà Phật — and the Japanese schools of Hōnen and Shinran made exclusive devotion to him the path of the person too burdened for self-power. In Tibet he presides over the red Buddha family; the phowa practice transfers consciousness to his Pure Land at death, and his longevity aspect Amitāyus crowns the long-life rituals. His cult also left traces far beyond Buddhism: Nestorian and Manichaean art along the Silk Road borrowed his radiance, the motif of light emanating from a divine face, and his welcoming descent shaped East Asian mortuary painting for a thousand years.
lore.culturalLegacy: Amitābha is one of the most widely invoked names in religious history: Namo Amituofo and Namu Amida Butsu have been recounted billions of times across East Asia, and Pure Land Buddhism remains among the largest forms of Buddhist practice worldwide. His image dominates temple halls from Kyoto to Xi'an; the Longmen and Dazu carvings give him mountains, and Hōryūji, Byōdōin, and Zenkōji give him houses. The Unicode restoration Amitābha preserves the long ā and aspirated bh that distinguish the Sanskrit original from every East Asian pronunciation of it — the name in the language in which the vows were first pronounced.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Amitābha is the Buddha who lowered the ladder. Where other paths ask the practitioner to climb by effort, he promised to reach down and lift up anyone who called his name. This is not weakness but a radical confidence in the power of compassion — and a frank diagnosis of the human condition: most people, most of the time, are too tired, too frightened, or too compromised to climb.

To recite Amitābha's name is to admit limitation and to trust grace at the same instant. It is the practice of the exhausted, the sinful, the busy, and the old — in other words, of nearly everyone. The light he radiates is not earned; it simply is, and the whole of the practice is to turn toward it. In this he stands close to the devotional hearts of other religions, yet his gift is unmistakably Buddhist: the Pure Land is not a final rest but a school, and birth there guarantees what self-power could not — the end of the curriculum.

sources.name: Hui Jiao, Gaoseng zhuan (Biographies of Eminent Monks)

lore.archaeology: The earliest artistic Amitābhas appear in Gandhāran and Mathuran sculpture of the early centuries CE, and his cult flourished along the Silk Road, leaving murals at Kizil and Dunhuang and colossal carvings at Longmen and Dazu in China. In East Asia his great houses are Hōryūji (Nara prefecture), Byōdōin at Uji (1053), and Zenkōji in Nagano — the last guarding a hidden seventh-century triad never shown to the public. Tibetan thangkas paint him red at the heart of the red family, flanked by Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, while the Lushan founding stones of Huiyuan's society survive in the mountain's inscriptions and the memory of Donglin monastery.
